key_terms.meaning: Split of fuel energy into brake power, heat to coolant, heat to exhaust and other losses; typically about 25–30% brake power, 30% coolant, 35% exhaust
Thin extended surface on an air-cooled cylinder or head that adds area for heat transfer to air by convection
Passages cast into the block and head around cylinders, valves and spark plug through which coolant flows
Natural circulation loop: hot, less dense coolant rises from the jacket to the radiator and cooler, denser coolant returns to the bottom of the jacket
A pump, usually centrifugal and belt driven, pushes coolant round the loop at a flow set by engine speed and thermostat opening
Spring-loaded radiator cap that holds the system above atmospheric pressure and so raises the boiling point: 100 kPa gauge lifts water from 100 °C to about 120 °C
Fluid that carries heat from the jacket to the radiator: water plus ethylene glycol for a lower freezing point and a higher boiling point, plus corrosion and scale inhibitors
FP = IP − BP, the power spent on rubbing surfaces and on pumping gas in and out; η<sub>m</sub> = BP/IP
Oil is stored in a pan at the bottom of the crankcase, drawn by a pump, filtered, fed to the bearings and drains back by gravity
Oil drains to a shallow pan, is scavenged to a separate tank and then pumped under pressure to the bearings; allows a low, flat engine and steady supply under cornering
Oil is mixed with petrol in a fixed ratio (often 1:50) for small two-strokes and lubricates every surface as the mixture passes through the crankcase
A number that shows how little an oil's viscosity changes with temperature; a higher VI means a flatter viscosity–temperature curve
Zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, an anti-wear and anti-oxidant additive that forms a protective film on rubbing metal surfaces
Gas leaking past the rings into the crankcase; the positive crankcase ventilation valve meters it, by manifold vacuum, into the intake to be burnt
A compressor driven mechanically from the crankshaft by belt, gear or chain that raises the density of the air entering the engine
ρ₂/ρ₁ = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂), with T₂ = T₁[1 + (r<sub>p</sub><sup>0.286</sup> − 1)/η<sub>c</sub>]
Gauge pressure of the intake air above atmospheric, for example 0.5 bar boost; boost ratio = p₂/p₁ absolute
An exhaust-gas turbine on one shaft with a centrifugal compressor; the turbine uses waste exhaust energy to drive the compressor
Delay between opening the throttle and getting full boost, caused by the time taken to build exhaust energy and spin the turbo up to speed
A turbo with movable vanes at the turbine inlet that close at low gas flow to keep gas speed high, and open at high flow to limit boost
A heat exchanger between the compressor and the intake manifold that cools compressed air, so its density and the trapped air mass rise
Replacing burnt gas in the cylinder with fresh charge in a two-stroke, driven by crankcase pressure or a separate blower through ports placed on the cylinder wall

key_terms.term: Delivery ratio, trapping and scavenging efficiency
key_terms.meaning: D = V<sub>del</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>; η<sub>t</sub> = V<sub>tr</sub>/V<sub>del</sub>; η<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>tr</sub>/V<sub>ec</sub>, all referred to the same pressure and temperature

takeaways: Only about a quarter to a third of the fuel energy leaves an engine as brake power; the rest must be taken away as heat by coolant, oil and exhaust.
Cooling must be controlled, not maximised: too little causes knock, pre-ignition and oil breakdown, while too much raises friction, wear and deposits and wastes fuel.
A thermosyphon loop drives only tens of pascals, so road engines use a pump; a pressure cap adds boiling margin (100 kPa gauge gives about 120 °C) but removes no heat itself.
Friction power changes little with load at a given speed, so mechanical efficiency is highest at full load and zero at idle; the right oil at the right pressure returns real brake power.
A lubricant is selected by its viscosity grade, viscosity index and additive package; the SAE 40 band is 12.5 to below 16.3 mm²/s at 100 °C.
Blow-by must be swept out of the crankcase and burnt: the PCV valve passes little at idle and most at full load.
Boost adds less air than its pressure ratio suggests, because compression heats the charge: 1.6 bar with a 0.70 efficient compressor gives only 1.33 times the density.
A turbocharger runs on exhaust energy that would otherwise be wasted, but its rotor must store ½Jω² before boost arrives; that delay is turbo lag.
Variable geometry fixes low-speed boost and the intercooler recovers the density lost to compressor heating, about 15 percent at 1.6 bar.
In a two-stroke the port layout decides how much fresh charge stays in the cylinder; uniflow and loop scavenging lose far less charge than simple cross flow.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually "explain with a neat sketch" questions: the cooling system layout, the lubrication circuit, the supercharger or turbocharger and its effects on performance. Most syllabi now also list crankcase ventilation and the properties of coolants, so expect a short question on each.

bank.q: Draw the heat balance of a petrol engine and explain why cooling is necessary. State what happens if the engine is overcooled.
outline: Typical split: 25–30% brake power, about 30% to coolant, about 35% out with exhaust, rest friction and radiation
Overheating effects: knock and pre-ignition, loss of volumetric efficiency, oil thinning and oxidation, thermal stress and warping of the head
Overcooling effects: higher friction and wear, poor fuel vaporisation, sludge and acid formation, lower thermal efficiency
Conclusion: cooling is a control problem, the jacket temperature must be held within a band
answer: Define the heat balance: an account, per second, of where the fuel energy goes. Fuel power = ṁ<sub>f</sub> × CV = brake power + heat to coolant + heat to exhaust + friction and radiation.

answer.text: Take a petrol engine burning 5 kg/h of fuel with CV = 44 000 kJ/kg. Fuel power = 5 × 44 000 ÷ 3600 = 61.1 kW. A typical split for a petrol engine:

answer: Draw the balance as a bar or a Sankey strip: one wide arrow of 61.1 kW splitting into the four streams above, the coolant stream labelled 18.3 kW. Figure 4.1.1 is the same picture for a diesel genset.

Why cooling is necessary (overheating): the gas passes 2000 °C while the cylinder wall must stay near 150 to 200 °C. Without cooling, (a) the oil film on the liner oxidises and cokes above about 150 °C at the rings, so rings stick and the liner scores; (b) aluminium pistons and heads lose strength, and the exhaust valve, already near 700 °C, burns; (c) hot spots cause pre-ignition and the hot charge raises knock in SI engines; (d) hot inlet walls heat the charge and lower volumetric efficiency; (e) uneven temperatures warp the head and blow the gasket.

Why it must not be overdone (overcooling): (a) petrol vaporises poorly on cold walls, so mixture and combustion worsen; (b) cold, thick oil raises friction and slows oil delivery, so wear rises; (c) water from combustion condenses in the crankcase with acids and forms sludge; (d) more heat goes to the coolant, so thermal efficiency and fuel economy fall; (e) emissions of unburnt HC rise.
The control that holds the band: the thermostat keeps coolant away from the radiator until about 80 to 90 °C, and the fan switches on only when needed.
Check: 17.1 + 18.3 + 20.8 + 4.9 = 61.1 kW, the whole fuel power. Conclusion: cooling removes roughly a third of the fuel energy and must hold the metal in a temperature band, neither hot nor cold.

bank.q: Compare air cooling and liquid cooling of IC engines with sketches, giving advantages, disadvantages and typical applications.
outline: Air cooling: fins on barrel and head, direct convection, no radiator or pump; needs a fan and ducting on multicylinder engines; local hot spots
Liquid cooling: water jacket, radiator, pump, thermostat, fan; uniform temperature, quieter, compact bore spacing
Comparison table on weight, cost, maintenance, cooling uniformity, warm-up, freezing risk
Applications: air for scooters, motorcycles, small gensets and aircraft; liquid for cars, trucks, tractors and large stationary engines
answer: Purpose of both: carry heat from the cylinder walls and head to the outside air. They differ in how the heat reaches the air.

svg.aria: Sketch: a finned air-cooled barrel with air flowing past the fins, and a liquid-cooled block with a jacket round the liner connected to a radiator.

answer: Air cooling: fins cast on the barrel and head add surface; air flows between them by road speed or a fan, guided by cowls and baffles; heat leaves by convection, Q = h A ΔT. Because h for air is small, a lot of area is needed: to reject 3.0 kW at h = 50 W/m²·K with fins at 160 °C in 35 °C air, A = 3000 ÷ (50 × 125) = 0.48 m², six times the 0.08 m² of the bare barrel and head.

Liquid cooling: coolant in a jacket picks up heat from the liner, valve seats and exhaust port; a belt-driven centrifugal pump sends it through the thermostat to the radiator; the fan pulls air through the radiator. Heat flow Q = ṁ c ΔT: a genset putting 28 kW into water that rises 6 K needs 28.0 ÷ (4.18 × 6) = 1.12 kg/s.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Point
Air cooling
Liquid cooling
rows: limited, hot spots at the head
high and even round all cylinders
jacket, pump, radiator, thermostat, fan, hoses

answer: Advantages of air cooling: simple, light, cheap, no coolant to freeze or leak, quick warm-up. Disadvantages: lower power per litre, uneven temperatures, noise, poor cooling in slow traffic or a closed room (in a 55 °C shed the same fins settle at 180 °C).

Advantages of liquid cooling: uniform temperature, higher compression ratio and power per litre possible, quieter, compact cylinder spacing, cabin heater from the coolant. Disadvantages: weight, cost, pump power, leaks and corrosion, more maintenance.
Applications: air for motorcycles, scooters, small pump sets and aircraft piston engines; liquid for cars, trucks, tractors, most gensets and large stationary engines.
Conclusion: air cooling trades power and temperature control for simplicity; liquid cooling is chosen wherever power per litre and even temperature matter.

bank.q: Explain the thermosyphon, forced circulation and pressure cooling systems. Why do modern engines use pressurised forced circulation?
outline: Thermosyphon: density difference drives flow, no pump, needs tall radiator, flow depends on temperature difference, slow warm-up circulation
Forced circulation: pump output, thermostat control, bypass during warm-up, higher flow and smaller radiator
Pressure cooling: sealed cap raises boiling point, a 100 kPa gauge cap lifts water from 100 °C to about 120 °C, so a higher jacket temperature is allowed with a smaller radiator and less fan power
Why: stable flow at all speeds, smaller and lighter radiator, no boiling at high altitude or high load
answer: All three are liquid cooling loops: jacket, radiator and connecting hoses. They differ in what drives the flow and at what pressure.

Thermosyphon: hot coolant in the jacket is lighter than cold coolant in the radiator. The hot riser rises to the radiator top tank, the cooled water falls through the downcomer to the jacket bottom. The driving pressure is Δp = (ρ<sub>c</sub> − ρ<sub>h</sub>) g h. Sketch: jacket low, radiator high, as Figure 4.2.1.

answer.text: Size of that pressure, with water at 80 °C in the riser (971.8 kg/m³), 40 °C in the downcomer (992.2 kg/m³) and h = 0.4 m:

answer: Consequences of so small a head: wide short pipes, a tall radiator well above the engine, no flow until the water is hot, and flow that falls exactly when the engine is cold or the radiator is clogged. Advantages: no pump, no power, simple. Used on small stationary engines.

Forced circulation: a belt-driven centrifugal pump adds tens of kPa, so flow is set by pump speed, not by temperature. A wax thermostat blocks the radiator until about 80 to 90 °C; a bypass lets the pump circulate through the jacket during warm-up; an expansion tank takes up volume changes. Flow is predictable at every speed, so the radiator is smaller.

Pressure cooling: a spring-loaded cap seals the system and holds it above atmospheric pressure. Saturation temperature rises with pressure, so the coolant can run hotter without boiling. The cap also carries a vacuum valve that lets coolant return from the overflow tank as the engine cools.

answer.text: Boiling points from the water tables, cap at 100 kPa gauge:

answer: Why modern engines use pressurised forced circulation: (a) flow is steady at all speeds and loads; (b) the coolant can run hotter, so the larger coolant-to-air temperature difference lets a smaller, lighter radiator and less fan power reject the same heat; (c) boiling is prevented on hill climbs, in traffic and at altitude, where an open system would boil at 93 °C; (d) coolant is not lost as steam.
Caution to state: never open a hot cap; the drop to atmospheric pressure flashes the coolant to steam.
Check: the cap does not remove heat; it buys boiling margin, here about 20 K above a 95 °C running temperature even at 2000 m.

bank.q: Explain the functions of engine lubrication and describe wet sump, dry sump and mist lubrication systems with sketches.
outline: Functions: reduce friction and wear, carry away heat, remove wear debris, seal piston rings, cushion shock loads, resist corrosion
Wet sump: strainer, gear pump, relief valve, filter, main gallery, drillings to mains, big ends, camshaft; oil returns by gravity
Dry sump: scavenge pump, remote tank, pressure pump; advantages in racing, aircraft and off-road vehicles
Mist: oil mixed with fuel, no pump or filter, total loss, used in small two-strokes
answer: Functions of lubrication: (1) reduce friction and wear by keeping a film between sliding parts; (2) cool the piston underside, bearings and turbo shaft; (3) seal the gap between rings and liner; (4) clean, carrying wear debris and soot to the filter; (5) cushion shock loads in bearings; (6) protect against rust and acid corrosion.
Classification by how the oil reaches the surface: mist (petroil), splash, and pressure feed; pressure-feed systems are wet sump or dry sump.

Wet sump, with a sketch as Figure 4.3.1: oil is stored in the sump under the crankcase. The pump (gear or rotor, driven from the crankshaft) draws it through the strainer, sends it through the full-flow filter (with a bypass valve if it clogs) to the main gallery, a drilled passage along the block. Drillings feed the main bearings, then through the crankshaft to the big ends, and to the camshaft bearings and rockers. Oil drains back to the sump by gravity. A relief valve next to the pump returns surplus oil to the sump so pressure cannot rise too high with cold, thick oil. Splash from the crank throws oil onto the liner and piston pin.

Advantages of wet sump: simple, cheap, compact; used in almost all cars and trucks. Limits: oil can surge away from the pick-up in hard cornering or on steep slopes, the deep sump raises engine height, and a small sump runs hot.

svg.aria: Dry sump circuit: oil drains from the bearings to a shallow pan, a scavenge pump lifts it to a separate tank, and a pressure pump feeds it through the filter and gallery back to the bearings.

answer: Dry sump working: oil drains to a shallow pan; a scavenge pump, larger than the pressure pump, lifts it to a separate tank; a pressure pump feeds the engine from the tank through the filter and gallery. Advantages: no oil surge in corners or on slopes, lower engine mounting and centre of gravity, larger and better-cooled oil volume. Disadvantages: two pumps, a tank and more piping, higher cost. Used in racing cars, aircraft and some off-road and heavy engines.

Mist (petroil) lubrication: oil mixed into the petrol at 1:50 to 1:20 (2 to 5 percent of the petrol volume) in crankcase-scavenged two-strokes. The mixture passes through the crankcase, the oil mist wets the bearings and cylinder, and the oil then burns. Advantages: no pump, filter or sump, works at any angle. Disadvantages: total loss of oil, smoke, plug fouling, oil supply tied to throttle and not to need. A four-stroke cannot use it because its crankcase never carries the fuel mixture.
Conclusion: pressure feed with a wet sump is the default; dry sump where oil surge or engine height matters; mist only in small two-strokes.

bank.q: Discuss the properties required of a lubricating oil and the additives used to obtain them.
outline: Viscosity and its SAE grade; viscosity index and multigrade oils
Pour point, flash point, fire point, cloud point, oiliness, film strength, volatility
Chemical stability: oxidation resistance, resistance to sludge and varnish
Additives: anti-wear (ZDDP), detergent and dispersant, anti-oxidant, pour-point depressant, VI improver, anti-foam, corrosion inhibitor, friction modifier
Why base oil alone cannot meet all requirements
answer: Why properties matter: oil must reach the bearings in a cold start, keep a film at full load and high temperature, and stay clean over thousands of kilometres. Each property is measured in a standard test.

answer.text: Physical properties:

head: Property
Meaning
Unit
rows: resistance to shear: dynamic μ, kinematic ν = μ/ρ
W part: cold cranking and pumping limits; hot part: ν band at 100 °C
how little ν falls with temperature
lowest temperature at which oil still flows
temperature at which wax makes it cloudy
friction and load capacity in boundary lubrication

answer.text: Worked check of viscosity: an oil at 100 °C has μ = 12.0 mPa·s and ρ = 840 kg/m³.

answer: Chemical properties: oxidation stability (resistance to acid, sludge and varnish formation); carbon residue (coke left on heating, in mass percent); total acid number TAN and total base number TBN, both in mg KOH/g (TAN rises and TBN falls as oil ages); demulsibility (separation from water); foaming resistance; low volatility to limit oil consumption.

answer.text: Additives and what each gives:

head: Additive
Function
rows: polymer that thickens hot oil more than cold: makes a multigrade
stops wax crystals joining into a gel
forms or reacts into a protective film on loaded contacts
keeps hot metal clean, neutralises acids (gives TBN)
keeps soot and sludge suspended so they drain out
breaks the oxidation chain that forms acid and sludge
coats metal against water and acid
breaks bubbles that would starve the pump
lowers boundary friction for fuel economy

answer: Why base oil alone is not enough: no base oil has a high enough VI, low enough pour point, detergency, acid neutralisation and anti-wear film all at once; additives, 1 to 20 percent by mass, supply what it lacks.
Conclusion: specify the oil by SAE grade for the climate, the maker's performance class, and an additive package matched to the engine (diesel soot, turbo heat, catalytic converter).

bank.q: Explain why an engine crankcase must be ventilated and describe the PCV system with a sketch. A 1.6 litre four-stroke engine runs at 2500 rev/min with volumetric efficiency 0.85 and its blow-by meter reads 20 L/min; find the blow-by as a percentage of intake air.
outline: Blow-by: what it is and what it contains
Effects of an unventilated crankcase: pressure, sludge, acid, oil dilution, pollution
Open road draft tube versus closed PCV system, with sketch
PCV valve operation at idle, part load, full load and backfire
Calculation: 1700 L/min of air, blow-by 1.18 percent
Turbo and diesel variants and common faults
answer: Blow-by: gas that leaks past the piston rings into the crankcase during compression and combustion. In a petrol engine it is unburnt mixture plus burnt gas: CO₂, H₂O, CO, NOx, fuel vapour, soot and oil mist.

Why ventilate: without a sweep of air, (a) crankcase pressure rises and pushes oil past seals and gaskets; (b) water vapour condenses on cold walls and forms sludge with oil and soot; (c) nitrogen and sulphur oxides form acids that corrode bearings; (d) fuel vapour dilutes and thins the oil; (e) if vented to the air, the hydrocarbons pollute.

Open system (road draft tube): a pipe from the crankcase to below the car, sucked by the air stream at road speed, with a breather cap for fresh air. It does nothing at idle and vents fuel vapour and oil mist to the air; emission rules ended it on petrol cars from the early 1960s.

Closed PCV system, with a sketch as Figure 4.5.1: filtered air from the clean side of the air cleaner enters the rocker cover, sweeps the crankcase, and the mixture of air and blow-by is drawn by manifold vacuum through an oil separator and the PCV valve into the intake manifold below the throttle, to be burnt. Surplus blow-by at full load flows back up the fresh-air hose to the air cleaner and is still burnt.

answer.text: PCV valve operation (tapered plunger, spring against manifold vacuum):
Calculation: a 1.6 litre four-stroke at 2500 rev/min, η<sub>v</sub> = 0.85, blow-by meter 20 L/min.
answer.pre:
V̇<sub>air</sub> = V<sub>d</sub> × N/2 × η<sub>v</sub> = 1.6 × 1250 × 0.85 = 1700 L/min
Blow-by fraction = 20 / 1700 × 100 = 1.18 %

answer: Turbocharged and diesel engines: under boost the manifold is above atmospheric, so a check valve shuts the PCV path and blow-by goes to the compressor inlet instead. Diesels, with no throttle vacuum, use a closed crankcase ventilation filter that removes oil and soot and sends the gas to the compressor inlet.

Faults: valve stuck open or split hose, unmetered air and a lean rough idle (10 kg/h measured plus 1.5 kg/h leak gives λ = 1.15); valve blocked, crankcase pressure, oil leaks, oil in the air cleaner and sludge.
Check: 1.18 percent is in the range of a healthy engine; a rising blow-by fraction at the same speed and load points to worn rings or liner.

bank.q: A four-stroke engine of 1.5 litre swept volume runs at 3000 rpm and gives indicated power 55 kW against brake power 40 kW. Find the friction power, the mechanical efficiency and the friction mean effective pressure.
outline: FP = IP − BP = 15 kW
Mechanical efficiency = BP/IP = 40/55 = 72.7%
Cycles per second = (3000/60)/2 = 25
fmep = FP/(V<sub>s</sub> × cycles per second) = 15000/(0.0015 × 25) = 4 × 10⁵ Pa = 4 bar
Comment on how fmep varies with speed and oil viscosity
answer: Given: V<sub>d</sub> = 1.5 L = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (whole engine), N = 3000 rev/min, IP = 55 kW, BP = 40 kW, four-stroke.

answer.text: Friction power:
Mechanical efficiency:
Cycles per second per cylinder for a four-stroke, and the swept volume handled per second:
Friction mean effective pressure:

answer: Check by the mean-effective-pressure route: imep = IP/(V<sub>d</sub> N/120) = 55 000/0.0375 = 14.7 bar and bmep = 40 000/0.0375 = 10.7 bar; imep − bmep = 4.0 bar = fmep, and bmep/imep = 0.727 = η<sub>m</sub>.

Comment on the value: 4 bar is high for a modern car engine at 3000 rev/min (motoring tests give nearer 1.5 to 2 bar, as in the 1.6 litre example of the lubrication chapter, 1.89 bar). It suggests the data includes pumping at part throttle or a worn engine.

How fmep varies: it rises with speed (bearing and ring shear grow with sliding speed, and pumping loss grows with flow), rises with oil viscosity (cold oil), and changes little with load at a fixed speed. That is why η<sub>m</sub> rises with load: FP stays near 15 kW while IP grows.

answer.text: What a lower fmep would be worth: if better oil and lower ring tension brought fmep down to 2.0 bar at the same speed and indicated power,

answer: How FP is measured in practice (named only; the methods belong to engine testing): motoring the engine with the fuel off, Willan's line (fuel rate against BP extended to zero load), the Morse test on a multi-cylinder engine, or IP from an indicator diagram minus BP from the dynamometer.
Why fmep is the better comparison: FP in kW grows with engine size and speed, while fmep is a pressure, so a 1.5 litre car engine and a 10 litre truck engine can be compared on the same scale.
Answer: FP = 15 kW, η<sub>m</sub> = 72.7 %, fmep = 4.0 bar.

bank.q: In a test, 30% of the fuel energy goes to the coolant. Fuel flow is 5 kg/h of calorific value 44 MJ/kg and the coolant water rises 8 °C. Find the coolant flow required in kg/s.
outline: Heat to coolant = 0.30 × 5 × 44000 kJ/h = 66000 kJ/h
Convert to kW: 66000/3600 = 18.3 kW
Q = m·c·ΔT with c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K
Comment on why real systems add a margin and use a thermostat and bypass
answer: Given: fuel 5 kg/h, CV = 44 MJ/kg = 44 000 kJ/kg, 30 % of the fuel energy to the coolant, coolant rise ΔT = 8 °C (8 K), water with c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K.

answer.text: Fuel energy per hour and per second:
answer.pre:
Fuel energy = 5 × 44 000 = 220 000 kJ/h
Fuel power  = 220 000 / 3600 = 61.1 kW

answer.text: Heat to the coolant:
Coolant flow from Q = ṁ c ΔT:

answer: Check: 0.548 × 4.18 × 8 = 18.33 kW, the coolant heat.
Unit care: c is in kJ/kg·K and Q in kW (kJ/s), so ṁ comes out in kg/s. Using 4180 J/kg·K with Q in kW would give an answer 1000 times too small.

Why real systems add a margin: the pump flow is set by engine speed, while the heat load peaks at full load and low road speed (hill climbs, traffic, high ambient); radiators lose capacity to scale, dirt and bent fins; glycol coolant has a lower specific heat than water (about 3.3 to 3.6 kJ/kg·K), so it needs more flow for the same rise. Designers size the pump and radiator for 20 percent or more above the calculated flow.

Why a thermostat and bypass are still needed: at light load or in cold weather the same flow would overcool the engine. The thermostat keeps coolant away from the radiator until the engine is warm, and the bypass keeps it circulating through the jacket meanwhile.

answer.text: Two follow-on checks the examiner may ask for: the air the radiator needs if the air warms by 20 K, and the coolant flow with 50 percent glycol (c ≈ 3.5 kJ/kg·K).
answer.pre:
ṁ<sub>air</sub> = 18.33 / (1.005 × 20) = 0.912 kg/s  (about 0.79 m³/s at 1.16 kg/m³)
ṁ<sub>glycol</sub> = 18.33 / (3.5 × 8) = 0.655 kg/s, about 20 % more than water

answer: Answer: about 0.548 kg/s of cooling water.

bank.q: A supercharger raises intake pressure from 1.0 bar to 1.6 bar absolute from 300 K. Treating compression as isentropic with γ = 1.4, find the delivery temperature and the density ratio.
outline: T₂ = T₁ (p₂/p₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup> = 300 × 1.6<sup>0.2857</sup>
Density ratio = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂) = 1.6 × 300/343 ≈ 1.40
So about 40% more air mass per cycle if volumetric efficiency stays the same
Note that real compression is not isentropic and a compressor efficiency of 0.7–0.8 must be used
answer: Given: p₁ = 1.0 bar, p₂ = 1.6 bar absolute, T₁ = 300 K, isentropic compression, γ = 1.4.

answer.text: Exponent and isentropic delivery temperature:
Density ratio from ρ = p/(RT):

answer: Meaning: about 40 percent more air mass per cycle at the same volumetric efficiency, not the 60 percent the pressure ratio suggests, because compression heats the air.

answer.text: Real compressor: with isentropic efficiency η<sub>c</sub> the temperature rise is larger.

answer: Effect on power: if power follows trapped air mass, a 75 kW engine would give 75 × 1.33 = 99.6 kW gross with a 0.70 efficient blower; a crank-driven blower then takes its drive power (7.15 kW in the supercharging worked example), leaving 92.4 kW net.
Check: 343.1 K is the lowest delivery temperature any compressor can reach at this ratio; a quoted delivery temperature below it is impossible.

answer.text: Work per kilogram of air and the power for 0.104 kg/s (the supercharging worked example's flow), with c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K:
Altitude compensation with the same blower at a hill town where p₁ = 0.795 bar and T₁ = 300 K (η<sub>c</sub> = 0.70, the temperature ratio is unchanged):
answer.pre:
p₂ = 1.6 × 0.795 = 1.272 bar, T₂ = 361.6 K
Density relative to sea-level ambient (1.0 bar, 300 K) = 1.272 × 300/361.6 = 1.055

answer: So at altitude the blower more than restores sea-level density, one of the stated objectives of supercharging.

Sketch to include: a p-v or T-s view of compression from state 1 (1.0 bar, 300 K) to state 2 (1.6 bar), with the ideal end point at 343 K and the real one to the right at 362 K; the gap is the extra work the inefficiency costs.
Answer: T₂ = 343 K and density ratio 1.40 for isentropic compression; about 1.33 with a real 0.70 efficient compressor.

bank.q: An intercooler cools the compressor delivery from 343 K to 313 K at almost constant pressure. Find the percentage rise in air density and explain the effect on engine power.
outline: At constant pressure, density ratio = T₂/T₃ = 343/313 = 1.096
About 9.6% more air mass in the same volume
With the same air–fuel ratio, about 9.6% more fuel can be burnt, so roughly the same rise in power
Also lower intake temperature reduces knock tendency, allowing a higher compression ratio or more boost
Note the pressure drop across the intercooler and its effectiveness
answer: Given: compressor delivery T₂ = 343 K, intercooler outlet T₃ = 313 K, pressure nearly constant through the cooler.

answer.text: At constant pressure ρ ∝ 1/T, so:
Effectiveness, if the cooling air enters at 303 K:

answer: Effect on air mass: the cylinder fills with 9.6 percent more air mass at the same boost and volumetric efficiency. With the same air-fuel ratio, 9.6 percent more fuel can be burnt, so power rises by roughly the same amount.
With the 1.6 bar boost from 300 K that gave 343 K, the overall density ratio becomes 1.6 × 300/313 = 1.53 instead of 1.40.

Further effects: (a) lower charge temperature lowers end-gas temperature, so knock falls in SI engines and more boost or a higher compression ratio can be used; (b) lower peak combustion temperature cuts NOx; (c) lower exhaust and component temperatures reduce thermal load on pistons and valves; (d) less fuel enrichment is needed for cooling at full load, so fuel consumption falls.
Penalties: the core loses some pressure, so the true gain is a little smaller; the extra volume adds to throttle lag; in a diesel too cold a charge lengthens the ignition delay.

answer.text: Heat the intercooler must reject, for an air flow of 0.10 kg/s:
answer.pre:
q = c<sub>p</sub> ΔT = 1.005 × (343 − 313) = 30.2 kJ/kg
Q = 0.10 × 30.2 = 3.0 kW to the cooling air

answer.text: Knock benefit in an SI engine, estimating the end-gas temperature after isentropic compression at compression ratio 9 (9<sup>0.4</sup> = 2.408):
answer.pre:
Without intercooler: 343 × 2.408 = 826 K
With intercooler:    313 × 2.408 = 754 K, about 72 K cooler

answer: Power example: an engine making 90 kW without the intercooler would make about 90 × 1.096 = 98.6 kW with it, at the same boost and air-fuel ratio, before allowing for the small pressure loss.
Answer: density rises 9.6 percent, giving about 9.6 percent more power at the same boost, plus a knock and NOx benefit.

bank.q: Explain turbo lag, its causes and the methods used to reduce it. Include variable geometry and intercooling in your answer.
outline: Cause: turbo speed depends on exhaust energy, which depends on fuel burnt; time constant of rotor inertia and gas build-up
Worse at low engine speed and after a gearshift; worse with a large turbo chosen for peak power
Remedies: small turbo, twin-scroll and divided turbine housing, lightweight compressor and turbine wheels, ball bearings, blow-off and wastegate control, VGT
VGT: vanes close at low flow to raise gas velocity and turbine work, open at high flow to avoid over-boost
Intercooling does not cut lag but raises the density benefit of the boost that does arrive
answer: Definition: turbo lag is the time between opening the throttle and getting full boost, at an engine speed where boost is possible. It differs from the boost threshold, which is the lowest engine speed at which the turbo can make any boost.

Causes: (1) the rotor (turbine wheel, shaft, compressor wheel) must store kinetic energy ½Jω² before it reaches boost speed; (2) exhaust energy rises only after more fuel is burnt, and more fuel needs more air, a loop that builds slowly; (3) the exhaust manifold and turbine housing volume must fill and pressurise; (4) the intake pipes and intercooler must fill with denser air; (5) a large turbine chosen for peak power gives low gas velocity at low flow.

answer.text: Numbers, from the turbocharging worked example: J = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg·m², spool from 30 000 to 150 000 rev/min with 1.8 kW of surplus turbine power.

answer: When it is worst: at low engine speed, after a gear change, and after light-load cruising, when exhaust energy is low and the rotor has slowed.

Remedies: (a) smaller turbine housing (higher gas velocity at low flow, but more back pressure at high flow); (b) twin-scroll or divided housings that keep exhaust pulses apart, and pulse rather than constant-pressure manifolds; (c) light wheels (titanium aluminide turbine, small compressor) and ball bearings instead of journal bearings to cut J and friction; (d) parallel twin turbos, each smaller, or sequential turbos with a small one for low speed; (e) electric assist on the shaft or an electric compressor; (f) variable geometry.

Variable geometry turbine: vanes round the turbine wheel close at low flow to narrow the throat and raise gas velocity, so the turbine makes more power early and spools fast; at high flow they open to lower back pressure and hold boost at the limit without a wastegate. It addresses lag and threshold together.

Intercooling: it does not cut lag, and its volume can add a little. It raises the density benefit of the boost that arrives: at 1.6 bar, cooling 361.6 K air to 314.7 K lifts the density ratio from 1.33 to 1.53.
Wastegate: it limits boost at high speed; it does not reduce lag, but it lets a smaller, quicker turbine be used without overboosting at the top end.
Conclusion: lag is an energy-storage delay; cut the energy to store (lighter rotor) or supply it faster (higher gas velocity, VGT, twin-scroll, electric assist).

bank.q: Compare supercharging and turbocharging. Discuss the effects of supercharging on engine power, knock, thermal loading and the modifications needed in the engine.
outline: Drive: mechanical (belt/gear) versus exhaust turbine; parasitic loss versus waste energy recovery
Response: immediate versus lag; boost curve against engine speed
Effect on power: power roughly proportional to air mass flow; volumetric efficiency and trapping efficiency change
Knock: higher intake temperature and pressure raise knock in SI engines; intercooling and retarded timing or lower compression ratio used
Thermal loading: higher gas temperature and pressure, hotter exhaust valve and piston; need for richer mixture at full load to cool the charge
Modifications: lower compression ratio, stronger pistons, connecting rods and bearings, better cooling and lubrication, sodium-cooled or better valve material, intercooler, boost control
answer: Both raise the air mass trapped per cycle so more fuel can be burnt in the same swept volume. They differ in where the compressor's power comes from.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Point
Supercharger
Turbocharger
rows: belt or gears from the crankshaft
exhaust gas turbine on a common shaft
lag of about 1 s, and a boost threshold
rises with exhaust energy; capped by wastegate or VGT
net gain reduced by drive power
hot turbine, oil and water feeds, heat soak

answer.text: Effect on power, with the supercharging worked example: 75 kW engine, 1.6 bar, 0.70 efficient blower.

answer: A turbocharger at the same boost takes its 5 kW or so of compressor power from the exhaust, so nearly all of the 99.6 kW reaches the crank, less a small rise in pumping work from turbine back pressure.

Effect on knock: boost raises both pressure and temperature of the end gas in SI engines, so knock tendency rises. Controls: intercooling, retarded spark, richer full-load mixture, lower compression ratio, higher-octane fuel, knock sensor.

Thermal loading: peak pressure and gas temperature rise, so pistons, rings, exhaust valves, head gasket and bearings carry more heat and load; more heat goes to the coolant and oil. In a CI engine the extra air usually lowers exhaust temperature at the same fuel rate.

answer.text: Modifications needed:

head: Part
Change
rows: stronger; piston alloy with lower thermal expansion; oil jets under the piston
larger radiator, oil cooler, turbo oil feed

answer: Evaluation: superchargers suit instant response and simple installation; turbochargers suit fuel economy and are now used on most boosted road engines, with VGT, twin-scroll housings or electric assist to hide lag.

bank.q: Compare cross-flow, loop and uniflow scavenging in two-stroke engines. Which gives the best scavenging efficiency and why?
outline: Cross: transfer and exhaust ports opposite, charge short-circuits to exhaust, poor scavenging efficiency, but simple
Loop (Schnürle): transfer ports angled to loop the charge up the back wall and over the head, pushing burnt gas out, used in most small petrol two-strokes
Uniflow: inlet ports at one end and exhaust valves or ports at the other, charge moves in one direction; best scavenging, needs a valve or opposed pistons
Compare scavenging efficiency, charging efficiency, charge loss and specific output
Also mention crankcase-scavenged versus blower-scavenged and the effect of exhaust tuning
answer: Scavenging replaces burnt gas with fresh charge while the ports are open near bottom dead centre. Measures: delivery ratio D = V<sub>del</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>, trapping efficiency η<sub>t</sub> = V<sub>tr</sub>/V<sub>del</sub>, scavenging efficiency η<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>tr</sub>/V<sub>ec</sub> and charging efficiency η<sub>t</sub> × D, all with volumes referred to the same pressure and temperature (they are really mass ratios).

Cross scavenging (sketch as Figure 4.9.1): transfer and exhaust ports on opposite walls; a deflector on the piston crown turns the charge up the transfer side, across under the head and down to the exhaust. Simple and cheap, but part of the charge short-circuits straight across, and the heavy deflector crown runs hot.

Loop (Schnürle) scavenging: transfer ports flank the exhaust and aim the charge at the far wall; the streams rise up that wall, turn over the head and sweep down to the exhaust. Flat piston crown, less short-circuiting, better trapping. Used in most small petrol two-strokes.

Uniflow scavenging: inlet ports round the bottom of the cylinder and an exhaust valve in the head (or ports uncovered by an opposed piston); the charge moves one way, inlet to exhaust, like a piston of air, with little mixing. Best scavenging, but needs a blower and valve gear or two crankshafts. Used in large marine and locomotive diesels.

answer.text: Worked comparison, D = 0.80, V<sub>ec</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> = 300 cm³, measured η<sub>t</sub> = 0.80:

answer: Reading the table: uniflow comes nearest the displacement line; loop lies between; cross flow, with short-circuiting, falls towards mixing or below it.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Type
Short-circuit
η<sub>s</sub>
Hardware
Use
rows: blower plus exhaust valve or opposed pistons

answer: Crankcase-scavenged engines (delivery ratio usually below 1, charge carries fuel and oil) lose fuel when charge short-circuits; blower-scavenged diesels lose only air. Tuned exhaust pipes return a pressure wave that pushes escaping charge back before the port closes.
Answer: uniflow gives the best scavenging efficiency because the flow never reverses or crosses itself, so fresh charge displaces burnt gas with least mixing and least short-circuiting.

bank.q: A small turbocharged petrol car is used mostly in stop-and-go Indian city traffic. Discuss the cooling, lubricant and boost-control choices you would make and why.
outline: Cooling: pressurised forced circulation with thermostat, electric fan that runs after shutdown to protect the turbo bearing, coolant with glycol and corrosion inhibitors
Lubrication: fully synthetic or semi-synthetic multigrade with high viscosity index, anti-wear and anti-oxidant additives, oil-cooled turbo bearing, short oil change interval for short trips
Turbo protection: idling before shutdown, oil feed from the main gallery with a restrictor and drain to the sump
Boost control: small turbo or VGT for early boost, intercooler to reduce knock at high ambient temperature, wastegate or electronic boost control
Trade-offs: fuel quality and knock, cost of synthetic oil against turbo life, heat soak in traffic
answer: The duty: short trips, long idling, low road speed and high ambient temperature (often 35 to 45 °C), occasional full-load bursts. The choices must handle heat soak, cold short-trip running, knock, and lag at low speed.

Cooling: pressurised forced circulation with a wax or map-controlled thermostat so the engine warms quickly on short trips; an electric fan that runs on after shutdown to cool the turbo and head; a 100 kPa cap so the coolant can run hot without boiling (120.4 °C at sea level); a 50 percent glycol coolant with corrosion inhibitors and distilled water, since scale from hard water cuts heat transfer; a water-cooled turbo bearing housing.

Lubrication: a low-viscosity, high-VI synthetic or semi-synthetic multigrade (for example 0W-20 or 5W-30 as the maker specifies) that flows at once on cold starts yet keeps its high-shear viscosity at the turbo bearing; strong antioxidant, detergent and anti-wear additives; shorter drain intervals than highway use, because short trips leave fuel and water in the oil. A turbo oil feed with a restrictor and a free drain back to the sump.

Crankcase ventilation: a closed PCV system with a good oil separator, routing blow-by to the compressor inlet under boost, so oil mist does not coat the compressor and intercooler. Short trips condense water in the crankcase; a working PCV sweep keeps sludge down.
Boost control: a small turbo, twin-scroll or VGT for boost from low speed, so the car pulls in traffic without lag; an electronically controlled wastegate; a knock sensor with spark retard.

answer.text: Intercooler at high ambient, 1.6 bar, η<sub>c</sub> = 0.70, air at 313 K (40 °C), ε = 0.80:

answer: Driver habits for the turbo: let it idle 30 to 60 seconds after a hard run before switching off, so oil carries heat away from the bearing housing.

Trade-offs: synthetic oil and short drain intervals cost more but protect the turbo bearing; a smaller turbo gives quick response but limits top-end power; running hotter coolant improves efficiency but narrows the knock margin, so the knock sensor and octane rating matter. Fuel quality varies, so the calibration must tolerate lower-octane petrol.

Conclusion: choose for heat and short trips first (pressurised cooling with after-run fan, high-VI synthetic oil, good PCV separation), then for low-speed boost with a small or variable geometry turbo and an intercooler sized for 40 °C air.

glossary.def: An account of where the chemical energy of the fuel goes: brake power, coolant, exhaust, friction and radiation.
A thin extended metal surface on an air-cooled engine that increases the area available for convection to air.
The set of cast passages in the block and head through which liquid coolant flows around hot parts.
A tube-and-fin heat exchanger that transfers heat from the coolant to the air stream.
A temperature-operated valve that keeps coolant away from the radiator until the engine reaches its working temperature.
Coolant circulation driven only by the density difference between hot and cold coolant, with no pump.
Coolant circulation produced by a pump, so the flow rate is set by pump speed and not by temperature alone.
The liquid used in a cooling system, normally water with ethylene glycol and corrosion inhibitors.
The internal resistance of a fluid to flow, quoted in centistokes (cSt) at a stated temperature or as an SAE grade.
A scale showing how much an oil's viscosity falls as temperature rises; higher index means less change.
The lowest temperature at which the oil will still flow under standard test conditions.
The temperature at which oil vapour gives a momentary flash when a flame is applied; a low value warns of fuel dilution.
A chemical blended into a base oil to give a property the base oil lacks, such as anti-wear or detergency.
A lubrication layout in which the oil supply sits in a pan under the crankshaft and drains back to it by gravity.
A lubrication layout in which oil is scavenged to a separate tank and pumped back under pressure to the engine.
Lubrication of small two-strokes by oil premixed with fuel, with no pump, filter or sump.
The difference between indicated power and brake power, spent on rubbing contacts and on pumping gas in and out of the cylinder.
The ratio of brake power to indicated power, η<sub>m</sub> = BP/IP.
A mechanically driven compressor that raises the pressure and density of the air entering the engine.
A turbine–compressor pair on a common shaft, where exhaust gas drives the turbine and the compressor boosts intake air.
The delay between a demand for power and the delivery of boost, set by rotor inertia and the time needed to build exhaust energy.
A heat exchanger that cools air leaving the compressor before it enters the intake manifold.
A turbocharger whose turbine inlet vanes move to match gas flow, giving high boost at low speed and safe boost at high speed.
The removal of burnt gas from a two-stroke cylinder and its replacement by fresh charge during the port overlap.
The first rush of high-pressure burnt gas out of the exhaust port when it opens, before fresh charge arrives.
The amount by which intake pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, usually quoted in bar.
Gas that leaks past the piston rings into the crankcase during compression and combustion.
A spring-loaded plunger valve that meters crankcase gas into the intake manifold according to manifold vacuum.
A valve that lets part of the exhaust bypass the turbine so that boost cannot rise above its set value.
